{{Short description|Embedding of categories into functor categories}}
The '''Yoneda lemma''' is a fundamental result in [[category theory]], a branch of mathematics.<ref name= riehl /> It is an abstract result on [[functor]]s of the type ''morphisms into a fixed object''. It is a vast generalisation of [[Cayley's theorem]] from [[group theory]] (viewing a group as a miniature category with just one object and only isomorphisms). It also generalizes the information-preserving relation between a term and its [[Continuation-passing style|continuation-passing style transformation]] from [[programming language theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boisseau |first=Guillaume |last2=Gibbons |first2=Jeremy |date=2018-07-30 |title=What you needa know about Yoneda: profunctor optics and the Yoneda lemma (functional pearl) |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3236779 |journal=Proc. ACM Program. Lang. |volume=2 |issue=ICFP |pages=84:1–84:27 |doi=10.1145/3236779|doi-access=free }}</ref> It allows the [[Subcategory#Embeddings|embedding]] of any [[locally small category]] into a [[category of functors]] ([[Functor#Covariance and contravariance|contravariant]] set-valued functors) defined on that category. It also clarifies how the embedded category of [[representable functor]]s and their [[natural transformation]]s relates to the other objects in the larger functor category. It is an important tool that underlies several modern developments in [[algebraic geometry]] and [[representation theory]]. It is named after [[Nobuo Yoneda]].

== Generalities ==

The Yoneda lemma suggests that instead of studying the [[locally small]] category <math> \mathcal{C} </math>, one should study the category of all functors of <math> \mathcal{C} </math> into <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> (the [[category of sets]] with [[function (mathematics)|functions]] as [[morphism]]s). <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> is a category we think we understand well, and a functor of <math> \mathcal{C} </math> into <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> can be seen as a "representation" of <math> \mathcal{C} </math> in terms of known structures. The original category <math> \mathcal{C} </math> is contained in this functor category, but new objects appear in the functor category, which were absent and "hidden" in <math> \mathcal{C} </math>. Treating these new objects just like the old ones often unifies and simplifies the theory.

This approach is akin to (and in fact generalizes) the common method of studying a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] by investigating the [[module (mathematics)|modules]] over that ring. The ring takes the place of the category <math> \mathcal{C} </math>, and the category of modules over the ring is a category of functors defined on <math> \mathcal{C} </math>.

== Formal statement ==

Yoneda's lemma concerns functors from a fixed category <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to a [[category of sets]], <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>. If <math> \mathcal{C} </math> is a [[locally small category]] (i.e. the [[hom-set]]s are actual sets and not [[proper class]]es), then each object <math> A </math> of <math> \mathcal{C} </math> gives rise to a functor to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> called a [[hom-functor]]. This functor is denoted:
:<math>h_A(-) \equiv \mathrm{Hom}(A,-)</math>.
The ([[Covariance and contravariance of functors|covariant]]) hom-functor <math> h_A </math> sends <math>X \in \mathcal{C}</math> to the set of [[morphism]]s <math> \mathrm{Hom}(A,X) </math> and sends a morphism <math> f \colon X \to Y </math> (where <math>Y \in \mathcal{C} </math>) to the morphism <math>f \circ -</math> (composition with <math>f</math> on the left) that sends a morphism <math>g</math> in <math> \mathrm{Hom}(A,X) </math> to the morphism <math>f \circ g</math> in <math> \mathrm{Hom}(A,Y)</math>. That is,
: <math>h_A(f) = \mathrm{Hom}(A,f), \text{ or}</math>
: <math>h_A(f)(g) = f \circ g</math>

Yoneda's lemma says that:

{{Math theorem|Let <math> F </math> be a functor from a locally small category <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>. Then for each object <math> A </math> of <math> \mathcal{C} </math>, the [[natural transformation]]s <math>\mathrm{Nat}(h_A,F)\equiv \mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Hom}(A,-),F)</math> from <math> h_A </math> to <math> F </math> are in one-to-one correspondence with the elements of <math> F(A) </math>; rather intuitively, there exists a bijection between <math>\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Hom}(A,-),F)</math> and <math>F(A)</math>. That is,
:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(h_A,F) \cong F(A)</math>
Moreover, this isomorphism is [[natural isomorphism|natural]] in <math>A</math> and <math>F</math> when both sides are regarded as functors from <math> \mathcal{C} \times \mathbf{Set}^\mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>.
| name = Lemma
| note = Yoneda
}}

Here the notation <math> \mathbf{Set}^\mathcal{C} </math> denotes the category of functors from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>.

Given a natural transformation <math>\Phi</math> from <math>h_A</math> to <math>F</math>, the corresponding element of <math>F(A)</math> is <math>u = \Phi_A(\mathrm{id}_A)</math>;{{efn|Recall that <math>\Phi_A : \mathrm{Hom}(A,A) \to F(A)</math> so the last expression is well-defined and sends a morphism from <math>A</math> to <math>A</math>, to an element in <math>F(A)</math>.}} and given an element <math>u</math> of <math>F(A)</math>, the corresponding natural transformation is given by <math>\Phi_{X}(f) = F(f)(u)</math> which assigns to a morphism <math>f \colon A \to X</math> a value of <math>F(X)</math>.

=== Contravariant version ===

There is a contravariant version of Yoneda's lemma,{{sfnp|Beurier|Pastor|2019|loc=Lemma 2.10 (Contravariant Yoneda lemma)}} which concerns [[contravariant functor]]s from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> (also known as [[Presheaf (category theory)|presheaves]]). This version involves the contravariant hom-functor
:<math>h^A(-) \equiv \mathrm{Hom}(-, A),</math>
which sends <math> X </math> to the hom-set <math> \mathrm{Hom}(X,A) </math>. Given an arbitrary contravariant functor <math> G </math> from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>, Yoneda's lemma asserts that
:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(h^A,G) \cong G(A).</math>

=== Naturality ===
The bijections provided in the (covariant) Yoneda lemma (for each <math>A</math> and <math>F</math>) are the components of a [[natural isomorphism]] between two certain functors from <math> \mathcal{C} \times \mathbf{Set}^\mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>.<ref name="Mac Lane">{{cite book|last=Mac Lane|first=Saunders|title=Categories for the working mathematician|language=en|edition=2|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|volume=5|publisher=Springer|location=New York, NY|date=1998|isbn=978-0-387-98403-2|issn=0072-5285|doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-4721-8|mr=1712872|zbl=0906.18001}}</ref>{{rp|61}} One of the two functors is the evaluation functor
:<math>-(-)\colon \mathcal{C} \times \mathbf{Set}^\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set} </math>
:<math>-(-)\colon (A,F)\mapsto F(A)</math>
that sends a pair <math>(f,\Phi)</math> of a morphism <math>f\colon A\to B</math> in <math>\mathcal C</math> and a [[natural transformation]] <math>\Phi\colon F\to G</math> to the map
:<math>\Phi_B\circ F(f)=G(f)\circ\Phi_A\colon F(A)\to G(B).</math>
This is enough to determine the other functor since we know what the natural isomorphism is. Under the second functor
:<math>\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(-,-),-)\colon\mathcal C\times\operatorname{Set}^{\mathcal C}\to\operatorname{Set},</math>
:<math>\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(-,-),-)\colon(A,F)\mapsto\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(A,-),F),</math>
the image of a pair <math>(f,\Phi)</math> is the map
:<math>\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(f,-),\Phi)=\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(B,-),\Phi)\circ\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(f,-),F)=\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(f,-),G)\circ\operatorname{Nat}(\hom(A,-),\Phi)</math>
that sends a natural transformation <math>\Psi\colon\hom(A,-)\to F</math> to the natural transformation <math>\Phi\circ\Psi\circ\hom(f,-)\colon\hom(B,-)\to G</math>, whose components are
:<math>(\Phi\circ\Psi\circ\hom(f,-))_C(g)=(\Phi\circ\Psi)_C(g\circ f)\qquad(g\colon B\to C).</math>

=== Naming conventions ===

The use of <math> h_A </math> for the covariant hom-functor and <math>h^A</math> for the contravariant hom-functor is not completely standard. Many texts<ref name="Vakil">{{cite book|last=Vakil|first=Ravi|title=The rising sea: Foundations of algebraic geometry|language=en|date=2026}}</ref> and articles either use the opposite convention or completely unrelated symbols for these two functors. [[Alexander Grothendieck]]'s foundational [[Éléments de géométrie algébrique|EGA]] also follows the opposite convention and defines <math> h_X(Y)=\operatorname{Hom}(Y,X) </math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Grothendieck
 |first1=Alexander
 |last2=Dieudonné
 |first2=Jean
 |title=Éléments de géométrie algébrique. III. Première partie
 |journal=Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS
 |volume=11
 |year=1961
 |pages=1–167
 |url=https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~leila.schneps/grothendieckcircle/EGA/EGAIII.1.pdf
}} In the opening page, Grothendieck introduces the notation
<math>h_X(Y)=\operatorname{Hom}(Y,X)</math>.</ref>{{efn|A notable exception to modern algebraic geometry texts following the conventions of this article is ''Commutative algebra with a view toward algebraic geometry'' / [[David Eisenbud]] (1995), which uses <math> h_A </math> to mean the covariant hom-functor. However, the later book ''The geometry of schemes'' / David Eisenbud, [[Joe Harris (mathematician)|Joe Harris]] (1998) reverses this and uses <math> h_A </math> to mean the contravariant hom-functor.}}
	

The mnemonic "falling into something" can be helpful in remembering that <math> h_A </math> is the covariant hom-functor. When the letter <math> A </math> is '''falling''' (i.e. a subscript), <math> h_A </math> assigns to an object <math> X </math> the morphisms from <math> A </math> '''into''' <math> X </math>.

=== Proof ===
Since <math>\Phi </math> is a natural transformation, we have the following [[commutative diagram]]:

[[File:Yoneda lemma cd.svg|center|Proof of Yoneda's lemma]]

This diagram shows that the natural transformation <math> \Phi </math> is completely determined by <math>\Phi_A(\mathrm{id}_A)=u</math> since for each morphism <math> f \colon A \to X </math> one has
:<math>\Phi_X(f) = (Ff)u.</math>
Moreover, any element <math> u \in F(A) </math> defines a natural transformation in this way. The proof in the contravariant case is completely analogous.<ref name="riehl">{{cite book|title=Category Theory in Context|last=Riehl|first=Emily|author-link=Emily Riehl|date=2017|publisher=Dover|isbn=978-0-486-82080-4|url=https://math.jhu.edu/~eriehl/161/context.pdf|archive-date=2019-12-14|access-date=2020-04-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214022210/http://www.math.jhu.edu/~eriehl/context.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== The Yoneda embedding ===

An important special case of Yoneda's lemma is when the functor <math>F</math> from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> is another hom-functor <math> h_B </math>. In this case, the covariant version of Yoneda's lemma states that
:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(h_A,h_B) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(B,A).</math>

That is, natural transformations between hom-functors are in one-to-one correspondence with morphisms (in the reverse direction) between the associated objects. Given a morphism <math> f \colon B \to A </math> the associated natural transformation is denoted <math> \mathrm{Hom}(f,-)</math>.

Mapping each object <math> A </math> in <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to its associated hom-functor <math> h_A  = \mathrm{Hom}(A,-) </math> and each morphism <math> f \colon B \to A </math> to the corresponding natural transformation <math> \mathrm{Hom}(f,-) </math> determines a contravariant functor <math>h_{\bullet}</math> from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set}^\mathcal{C} </math>, the [[functor category]] of all (covariant) functors from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>. One can interpret <math>h_{\bullet}</math> as a [[covariant functor]]:
:<math>h_{\bullet}\colon \mathcal{C}^{\text{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}^\mathcal{C}.</math>
The meaning of Yoneda's lemma in this setting is that the functor <math> h_{\bullet} </math> is [[full and faithful functors|fully faithful]], and therefore gives an embedding of <math> \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}} </math> in the category of functors to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>. The collection of all functors <math> \{h_A | A \in C\}</math> is a subcategory of <math> \mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{C}} </math>. Therefore, Yoneda embedding implies that the category <math> \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}} </math> is [[isomorphism of categories|isomorphic]] to the category <math>\{h_A | A \in C \}</math>.

The contravariant version of Yoneda's lemma states that
:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(h^A,h^B) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(A,B).</math>
Therefore, <math> h^{\bullet} </math> gives rise to a covariant functor from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to the category of contravariant functors to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math>:
:<math>h^{\bullet}\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}}.</math>
Yoneda's lemma then states that any locally small category <math> \mathcal{C} </math> can be embedded in the category of contravariant functors from <math> \mathcal{C} </math> to <math> \mathbf{Set} </math> via <math>h^{\bullet}</math>. This is called the ''Yoneda embedding''.

The Yoneda embedding is sometimes denoted by よ, the [[hiragana]] [[Yo (kana)|Yo]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Yoneda+embedding#ReferencesNotation | title=Yoneda embedding | website=nLab |access-date=6 July 2019 }}</ref>

=== Representable functor ===
{{Main|Representable functor}}
The Yoneda embedding essentially states that for every (locally small) category, objects in that category can be [[Representable functor|represented]] by [[Presheaf (category theory)|presheaves]], in a full and faithful manner.  That is,
:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(h^A,P) \cong P(A)</math>
for a presheaf ''P''.  Many common categories are, in fact, categories of pre-sheaves, and on closer inspection, prove to be categories of [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]], and as such examples are commonly topological in nature, they can be seen to be [[topoi]] in general. The Yoneda lemma provides a point of leverage by which the topological structure of a category can be studied and understood.

=== In terms of (co)end calculus ===
{{Main|End (category theory)}}

Given two categories <math>\mathbf{C}</math> and <math>\mathbf{D}</math> with two functors <math>F, G : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}</math>, natural transformations between them can be written as the following [[End (category theory)|end]].{{sfnp|Loregian|2021|loc=Theorem 1.4.1}}

:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(F, G) = \int_{c \in \mathbf{C}} \mathrm{Hom}_\mathbf{D}(Fc, Gc)</math>

For any functors <math>K \colon \mathbf{C}^{op} \to \mathbf{Set}</math> and <math>H \colon \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{Set}</math> the following formulas are all formulations of the Yoneda lemma.{{sfnp|Loregian|2021|loc=Proposition 2.2.1 (Ninja Yoneda Lemma)}}

:<math>
K \cong \int^{c \in \mathbf{C}} Kc \times \mathrm{Hom}_\mathbf{C}(-,c),
\qquad
K \cong \int_{c \in \mathbf{C}} (Kc)^{\mathrm{Hom}_\mathbf{C}(c,-)},
</math>

:<math>
H \cong \int^{c \in \mathbf{C}} Hc \times \mathrm{Hom}_\mathbf{C}(c,-),
\qquad
H \cong \int_{c \in \mathbf{C}} (Hc)^{\mathrm{Hom}_\mathbf{C}(-,c)}.
</math>

===Yoneda extension===
[[File:Yoneda extension.svg|thumb|Yoneda extension]]
Let <math>\mathcal{C}</math> be a small category,  <math>F:\mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathcal{D}</math> a functor, and <math>[\mathcal{C}^{op}, \mathbf{Set}]</math> the [[category of presheaves]], its Yoneda extension<ref>{{harvnb|Loregian|2021|loc=3.1.1 Overture: the universal property of <math>[\mathcal{C}^{op}, \mathbf{Set}]</math>}}</ref>

<math>\tilde F:[\mathcal{C}^{op}, \mathbf{Set}] \rightarrow \mathcal{D}</math>

is the left [[Kan extension]] <math>\mathrm{Lan}_{H^{\bullet}} F:[\mathcal{C}^{op},\mathbf{Set}] \rightarrow \mathcal{D}</math> of <math>F</math> along the Yoneda embedding <math>H^{\bullet}</math>:

<math>\tilde F :=\mathrm{Lan}_{H^{\bullet}} F</math>

== Preadditive categories, rings and modules ==
{{Main|Preadditive category}}

A ''[[preadditive category]]'' is a category where the morphism sets form [[abelian group]]s and the composition of morphisms is [[bilinear operator|bilinear]]; examples are categories of abelian groups or modules. In a preadditive category, there is both a "multiplication" and an "addition" of morphisms, which is why preadditive categories are viewed as generalizations of [[ring (mathematics)|rings]]. Rings are preadditive categories with one object.

The Yoneda lemma remains true for preadditive categories if we choose as our extension the category of ''[[additive functor|additive]]'' contravariant functors from the original category into the category of abelian groups; these are functors which are compatible with the addition of morphisms and should be thought of as forming a ''[[module category]]'' over the original category. The Yoneda lemma then yields the natural procedure to enlarge a preadditive category so that the enlarged version remains preadditive — in fact, the enlarged version is an [[abelian category]], a much more powerful condition. In the case of a ring <math>R</math>, the extended category is the category of all right [[module (mathematics)|modules]] over <math>R</math>, and the statement of the Yoneda lemma reduces to the well-known isomorphism
:<math> M \cong \mathrm{Hom}_R(R,M)</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;for all right modules <math>M</math> over <math>R</math>.

== Relationship to Cayley's theorem ==
As stated above, the Yoneda lemma may be considered as a vast generalization of [[Cayley's theorem]] from [[group theory]]. To see this, let <math> \mathcal{C} </math> be a category with a single object <math>*</math> such that every morphism is an [[isomorphism]] (i.e. a [[groupoid]] with one object). Then <math>G=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(*,*)</math> forms a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] under the operation of composition, and any group can be realized as a category in this way.

In this context, a covariant functor <math> \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set} </math> consists of a set <math>X</math> and a [[group homomorphism]] <math>G\to\mathrm{Perm}(X)</math>, where <math>\mathrm{Perm}(X)</math> is the group of [[permutation]]s of <math>X</math>; in other words, <math>X</math> is a [[G-set]]. A natural transformation between such functors is the same thing as an [[equivariant map]] between <math>G</math>-sets: a set function <math>\alpha \colon X \to Y</math> with the property that <math>\alpha(g\cdot x)=g\cdot\alpha(x)</math> for all <math>g</math> in <math>G</math> and <math>x</math> in <math>X</math>. (On the left side of this equation, the <math> \cdot </math> denotes the action of <math>G</math> on <math>X</math>, and on the right side the action on <math>Y</math>.)

Now the covariant hom-functor <math>\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(*,-)</math> corresponds to the action of <math>G</math> on itself by left-multiplication (the contravariant version corresponds to right-multiplication). The Yoneda lemma with <math>F=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(*,-)</math> states that
:<math>\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(*,-),\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(*,-)) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(*,*)</math>,
that is, the equivariant maps from this <math>G</math>-set to itself are in bijection with <math>G</math>. But it is easy to see that (1) these maps form a group under composition, which is a [[subgroup]] of <math>\mathrm{Perm}(G)</math>, and (2) the function which gives the bijection is a group homomorphism. (Going in the reverse direction, it associates to every <math>g</math> in <math>G</math> the equivariant map of right-multiplication by <math>g</math>.) Thus <math>G</math> is isomorphic to a subgroup of <math>\mathrm{Perm}(G)</math>, which is the statement of Cayley's theorem.

== History ==

Yoshiki Kinoshita stated in 1996 that the term "Yoneda lemma" was coined by [[Saunders Mac Lane]] following an interview he had with Yoneda in the [[Gare du Nord]] station.<ref>{{cite web|title=Prof. Nobuo Yoneda passed away|last=Kinoshita|first=Yoshiki|url=http://www.mta.ca/~cat-dist/catlist/1999/yoneda|access-date=21 December 2013|date=23 April 1996}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|access-date=2022-09-10|title=le lemme de la Gare du Nord |website= neverendingbooks|url=http://www.neverendingbooks.org/le-lemme-de-la-gare-du-nord| date=18 November 2016}}</ref>
